subject: english
stem: According to the passage, how do mangroves cope with mud that holds very little oxygen?

options.text: Their roots grow upward out of the mud and draw in air.
Their leaves absorb oxygen from the mud through special glands.
Their roots store oxygen at high tide for use later.
Their roots grow deep below the mud to reach oxygen.

explanation: The first paragraph says the arching roots rise above the surface and take in air, so part of the breathing is done in the open. The glands mentioned in option B push out salt, not oxygen. Options C and D are not stated in the passage.
passage_text:
Along tropical coastlines, where rivers meet the sea, grow forests that seem to stand on stilts. These are mangroves, trees that have adapted to live in salty, waterlogged mud where most plants would die. Their arching roots rise above the surface and take in air, while in some species special glands in the leaves push out excess salt. Because the mud holds very little oxygen, the roots do part of their breathing in the open air.

For coastal communities, mangroves are a living defence. Their tangled roots slow the incoming waves and hold the soil together, so that the shore is worn away more slowly during storms. After the tsunami of 2004, several studies suggested that villages sheltered behind dense mangrove belts suffered less damage than those along bare beaches. The roots do not stop a giant wave entirely, but they take away a good part of its force.

Mangroves are also nurseries. Young fish, crabs and prawns shelter among the roots, safe from larger predators, before moving into open water. Many fishing families depend on these catches, and honey collectors and wood cutters earn a modest living from the forest as well.

Despite this value, mangroves have been cleared in large numbers to make way for shrimp farms, ports and hotels. A large share of the world's mangroves has disappeared in recent decades. Conservation groups now encourage local villagers to replant saplings, but they warn that planting alone is not enough: the seedlings survive only if the tides and the flow of fresh water are first restored to the site.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 English, Vistas Ch. 3 'Journey to the End of the Earth' (environment and climate theme); Reading Comprehension, unseen factual passage, skill: detail

subject: english
stem: Which of the following best describes Nila's state of mind when she reaches the school gate?

options.text: Angry that her father had moved the family
Confident and keen to meet new friends
Nervous and out of place among strangers
Bored by the crowd of unfamiliar faces

explanation: Nila clutches her bag, looks for an empty bench and pretends to search her pencil box, all signs of nervousness in a place where she feels she is nobody. Nothing suggests anger, confidence or boredom.
passage_text:
Nila had practised the walk to the bus stop for three days, but on the first morning of her new school her legs felt like someone else's. Her father had been transferred to the city in June, and the small town where everyone knew her name was now a three-hour train ride behind them. In the city, she was nobody.

At the school gate, girls in crisp uniforms stood in tight circles, laughing at jokes that she could not follow. Nila clutched her bag and looked for an empty bench. She found one beneath a gulmohar tree and sat down, pretending to search for something important in her pencil box. When the bell rang, she felt both relieved and ashamed of the relief.

In the classroom the teacher asked each student to say what she wanted to become. Answers came quickly: doctor, pilot, cricketer. Nila's mouth went dry. At home she had always said she wanted to be a mapmaker, but here the word seemed too odd, even a little ridiculous. When her turn came, she stood up, opened her mouth, and heard herself say, "A mapmaker."

Nobody laughed. The teacher raised her eyebrows with interest, and a girl in the third row turned around and whispered, "Can you draw our school?" Nila nodded, surprised at how steady her voice sounded. At lunch the same girl pulled her into one of the tight circles, handed her a pen and a folded sheet of paper, and said, "Start with the gate."

That evening her father asked how the day had gone. "Short," said Nila, and smiled, because it had begun as the longest morning of her life.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 English, Flamingo Prose 'Going Places' (adolescent aspiration and self-doubt); Reading Comprehension, unseen narrative passage, skill: detail

subject: english
stem: The central idea of the passage is that

options.text: people must abandon clocks, schedules and work to find peace of mind
farmers and potters lead better lives than people who live in busy cities
poets are wiser than ordinary people because they work slowly and quietly
daily moments of stillness bring clarity and self-understanding in a hurried world

explanation: The author asks for a few minutes of pause each day so that the mind can settle and the person within can be met. Option A is rejected in the third paragraph, and options B and C are only supporting examples turned into false claims.
passage_text:
We are a people in a hurry. Trains are announced before they leave, messages are answered before they are fully read, and even our holidays arrive with a schedule pinned to them. Somewhere along the way, we began to treat stillness as a kind of waste, as though a minute not spent doing something were a minute stolen from us.

Yet the things that matter most to us have rarely been produced in a rush. A farmer waits through a whole season for the grain to ripen. A potter must let the clay dry slowly, for if it is hurried it cracks in the fire. Even a friendship worth keeping needs long afternoons in which nothing in particular happens. The poets have always known this. They sit by a window, watch the light travel across a wall, and somehow return with a line that is more true than a hundred busy speeches.

I do not suggest that we should give up our clocks or our work. I am only asking for a small rebellion: a few minutes each day in which we count nothing and chase nothing. In that pause, the mind, like a pond left alone, settles, and what was muddy slowly grows clear. We may even find, to our surprise, that the noise we blamed on the world was largely our own.

It is a modest gift to give oneself, and it costs nothing. But it requires courage, because in stillness we must meet the person we have been hurrying away from.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 English, Flamingo Poetry Ch. 2 'Keeping Quiet' (stillness and reflection); Reading Comprehension, unseen literary passage, skill: central idea

stem: The Mature Harappan phase of the Indus Valley Civilisation is generally dated to about:
explanation: NCERT places the Mature Harappan phase between about 2600 and 1900 BCE. The Early Harappan cultures came before it, and the Late Harappan cultures followed the decline of the cities after about 1900 BCE.

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem: Faience, which the Harappans used for small vessels and ornaments, was prepared by:

options.text: firing a mixture of clay, powdered shell and dung in a kiln
melting copper with tin and pouring the molten metal into moulds
heating steatite until it hardened and acquired a natural glaze
firing a paste of ground sand or silica mixed with colour and a gum

explanation: NCERT defines faience as a material made by firing a paste of ground sand or silica mixed with colour and a gum. Heating steatite, casting bronze and firing clay are separate Harappan techniques and do not produce faience.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 1 (Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation), section 'Making sense of social differences' (faience as a luxury item)

stem:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Shortughai
(B) Khetri
(C) Dilmun
(D) Meluhha

List-II
(I) Island region usually identified with Bahrain
(II) Harappan trading post in Afghanistan, near a source of lapis lazuli
(III) Region of Rajasthan that supplied copper
(IV) Mesopotamian name for the Harappan region

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Shortughai in Afghanistan lay near the best source of lapis lazuli, and the Khetri region of Rajasthan supplied copper. Mesopotamian texts name Dilmun (probably Bahrain) and call the Harappan region Meluhha.

stem:
Which of the following statements about Harappan urban planning are correct?

(A) The settlement was often divided into a smaller, higher citadel and a larger, lower town.
(B) Sun-dried and baked bricks alike were made in a uniform ratio, with length, breadth and height in the proportion 4:2:1.
(C) Houses at Mohenjodaro were built first, and drains and streets were laid out afterwards.
(D) Many houses had a bathing area whose waste water flowed into drains along the street.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Statements (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Statement (C) is wrong because the drains and streets appear to have been laid out first, with houses then built along them.

stem: The Brahmi script used in most inscriptions of Ashoka was deciphered in 1838 by:
explanation: James Prinsep, an officer of the East India Company's mint, deciphered the Brahmi script of Ashoka's inscriptions in 1838. This also showed that the king named in them, Devanampiya Piyadassi, was Ashoka.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 2 (Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies), section 'Prinsep and Piyadassi'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem: Which of the following was NOT a provincial centre of the Mauryan empire?
explanation: The Mauryan empire had five major political centres: the capital Pataliputra and the provincial centres of Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri. Mathura is not in this list.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 2 (Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies), section 'An early empire' (the Mauryan empire)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem:
Which of the following statements about the inscriptions of Ashoka are correct?

(A) Most of them were composed in Prakrit.
(B) All of them were written in Sanskrit.
(C) In the north-west, Kharosthi was used as the script.
(D) In Afghanistan, some were written in Greek and Aramaic.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Ashoka's inscriptions were mostly in Prakrit and written in Brahmi, with Kharosthi in the north-west and Greek and Aramaic in Afghanistan. Statement (B) is wrong because they were not written in Sanskrit.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 2 (Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies), sections 'Prinsep and Piyadassi' and 'An early empire'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Gotami-putra Siri-Satakani
(B) Samudragupta
(C) Rudradaman
(D) Prabhavati Gupta

List-II
(I) Vakataka queen and daughter of Chandragupta II
(II) Ruler eulogised in the Prayaga Prashasti
(III) Satavahana ruler known by a name derived from his mother
(IV) Ruler whose Junagadh inscription records the repair of the Sudarshana lake

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Gotami-putra Siri-Satakani was a Satavahana ruler named through his mother, and Samudragupta is praised in the Prayaga Prashasti. Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription records the repair of the Sudarshana lake, and Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, married a Vakataka ruler.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 2 (Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies), sections 'Kings and kingdoms', 'Land grants and peasants' and 'Irrigation'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem:
Arrange the following rulers in chronological order, from the earliest to the latest.

(A) Chandragupta Maurya
(B) Samudragupta
(C) Gautamiputra Satakarni
(D) Bimbisara

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Bimbisara of Magadha belongs to the sixth century BCE, and Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan empire around 321 BCE. The Satavahana ruler Gautamiputra Satakarni came in the early centuries CE, and Samudragupta of the Gupta dynasty ruled in the fourth century CE.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 2 (Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies), sections 'The earliest states', 'An early empire' and 'Kings and kingdoms'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem: In early Pali texts, the term gahapati was used for:

options.text: the village headman who collected taxes on behalf of the king
the head of a household who controlled its land and animals
a merchant belonging to a guild of traders known as a shreni
a landless labourer who worked on the king's own farmland

explanation: Gahapati meant the head of a household who controlled the family's resources, such as land and animals, and exercised authority over the women, slaves and workers of the household. The village headman was the grama-bhojaka, a different figure.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 2 (Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies), section 'Changes in agriculture' (Pali texts on villagers)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem: Which of the following mahajanapadas was ruled by a gana or sangha, an oligarchy of many rulers, rather than by a single king?
explanation: Vajji was a gana or sangha, in which power was held jointly by a group of rajas. Magadha, Kosala and Avanti were monarchies.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 2 (Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies), section 'The earliest states' (mahajanapadas)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem: Brahmanical texts laid down the rule of gotra exogamy. It meant that:

options.text: a man and a woman of the same gotra could not marry each other
marriage had to take place only between members of the same gotra
a woman continued to belong to her father's gotra after marriage
a man could marry only a woman of his own varna and gotra

explanation: Gotra exogamy forbade marriage between persons of the same gotra. Brahmanical texts also said that a woman should give up her father's gotra and adopt her husband's gotra after marriage.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 3 (Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies), section 'Rules of marriage' (Kinship and marriage)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Polyandry
(B) Endogamy
(C) Exogamy
(D) Polygyny

List-II
(I) Marriage outside a unit such as a gotra or kin group
(II) Marriage within a unit such as a caste or kin group
(III) A woman having several husbands
(IV) A man having several wives

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Polyandry is one woman with several husbands, and polygyny is one man with several wives. Endogamy is marriage within a defined group, and exogamy is marriage outside it.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 3 (Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies), section 'Rules of marriage' (polygyny, polyandry, endogamy and exogamy)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem:
Consider the following statements about kinship and marriage in early societies (c. 600 BCE to 600 CE):
(A) Brahmanas classified themselves into gotras, each named after a Vedic seer.
(B) After marriage, a woman was expected to give up her father's gotra and adopt that of her husband.
(C) Marriage between members of the same gotra was the accepted norm.
(D) Several Satavahana rulers were identified through names derived from their mothers.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: From about 1000 BCE Brahmanas were classified into gotras named after Vedic seers, and women adopted their husband's gotra after marriage. Members of the same gotra could not marry each other, so statement (C) is false. Satavahana rulers used metronymics such as Gotami-putra, so (D) is true.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 3 (Kinship, Caste and Class), section 'Kinship and marriage: many rules and varied practices'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I (Term)
(A) Patriliny
(B) Exogamy
(C) Endogamy
(D) Polygyny
List-II (Meaning)
(I) Marriage outside the kin group or gotra
(II) Tracing descent through the father's line
(III) Marriage within a group such as a caste or a locality
(IV) Practice of having several wives
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Patriliny means descent traced through the father's line. Exogamy is marriage outside the unit (kin group or gotra) and endogamy is marriage within a unit such as a caste. Polygyny is the practice of a man having several wives.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 3 (Kinship, Caste and Class), section 'Kinship and marriage: many rules and varied practices' and glossary terms

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem: Which part of the Buddhist Tripitaka contains the rules and regulations for those who joined the sangha?
explanation: The Tripitaka has three Pitakas. The Vinaya Pitaka lays down rules for the sangha, the Sutta Pitaka holds the Buddha's teachings, and the Abhidhamma Pitaka deals with philosophical matters.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 4 (Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings), section on the teachings of the Buddha and Buddhist texts

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem:
Arrange the following parts of a stupa in order, from the base upwards.
(A) Yashti
(B) Anda
(C) Chhatri
(D) Harmika
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: A stupa begins with a hemispherical mound called the anda. Above it stands the harmika, a balcony-like structure representing the abode of the gods. A mast called the yashti rises from the harmika and is topped by a chhatri or umbrella.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 4 (Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings), section on stupas (the structure of the stupa)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem:
Consider the following statements about Jainism:
(A) Mahavira was the first of the twenty-four tirthankaras.
(B) The entire world is believed to be animate, so even stones, rocks and water have life.
(C) Non-injury to humans, animals, plants and insects is central to Jaina teaching.
(D) The cycle of birth and rebirth is shaped through karma.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Jaina philosophy holds that the whole world is animate and stresses ahimsa. It teaches that karma shapes the cycle of birth and rebirth. Mahavira was the last, not the first, of the twenty-four tirthankaras, so (A) is false.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 4 (Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings), section 'Beyond worldly pleasures: the message of Mahavira'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
stem: The idea of the Buddha as a saviour, along with the worship of his images, developed in which Buddhist tradition?
explanation: In the early tradition the Buddha was represented through symbols. With the emergence of Mahayana Buddhism the Buddha came to be seen as a saviour, and his images began to be made and worshipped. The older tradition (Theravada, also called Hinayana by Mahayana followers) did not develop this idea, and Digambara is a sect of Jainism, not Buddhism.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 4 (Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings), section on the Buddha's teachings and the later Buddhist traditions (Mahayana)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind was written in which language?
explanation: Al-Biruni wrote the Kitab-ul-Hind in Arabic. Written in the eleventh century, it is a large work divided into 80 chapters on subjects such as religion, philosophy, festivals, astronomy, manners and customs.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 5 (Through the Eyes of Travellers), section 'Al-Biruni and the Kitab-ul-Hind'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: Which Sultan, impressed by Ibn Battuta's scholarship, appointed him the qazi (judge) of Delhi?
explanation: Ibn Battuta reached Sind in 1333. Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq was impressed by his learning and appointed him qazi of Delhi, a post he held for several years.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 5 (Through the Eyes of Travellers), section on Ibn Battuta's Rihla

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem:
Consider the following statements about François Bernier:
(A) He regarded the crown's ownership of all land as beneficial to peasants and to the state.
(B) He described Mughal cities as 'camp towns'.
(C) He was a French physician who spent several years in Mughal India.
(D) He described Mughal society as having a large and prosperous middle class.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Bernier was a French doctor who travelled in Mughal India. He called Mughal cities 'camp towns' that depended on the imperial camp. He believed that crown ownership of land and the absence of private property harmed peasants and the state, and he saw society as a few rich people ruling a vast multitude of poor, so (A) and (D) are false.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 5 (Through the Eyes of Travellers), section 'Francois Bernier: a doctor with a difference'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: Which aspect of the caste system did Al-Biruni disapprove of, arguing that it was contrary to the laws of nature?

options.text: The division of society into four varnas
The hereditary status of Brahmanas as priests
The practice of marrying within one's own caste

explanation: Al-Biruni accepted the Brahmanical description of the caste system and tried to explain it through parallels with ancient Persian social classes. He disapproved of the notion of pollution, arguing that everything impure strives to regain its original state of purity, as the sun cleanses the air.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 5 (Through the Eyes of Travellers), section on Al-Biruni and the Sanskritic tradition (understanding the caste system)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem:
Arrange the following travellers in the chronological order of their visits to the Indian subcontinent, earliest first.
(A) François Bernier
(B) Al-Biruni
(C) Abdur Razzaq
(D) Ibn Battuta
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Al-Biruni came in the early eleventh century with the armies of Mahmud of Ghazni. Ibn Battuta reached India in 1333, Abdur Razzaq of Samarqand visited Calicut and Vijayanagara in the 1440s, and Bernier travelled in Mughal India from 1656 to 1668.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 5 (Through the Eyes of Travellers), introductory section; Part II Theme 7 (Abdur Razzaq at Vijayanagara)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: The compositions of the Nayanars, the Shaiva saints of the Tamil country, were compiled in which collection?
explanation: The Nayanars were devotees of Shiva and their hymns were compiled as the Tevaram. The compositions of the Alvars, devotees of Vishnu, were compiled in the Nalayira Divyaprabandham.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6 (Bhakti-Sufi Traditions), section on the Alvars and Nayanars (Tamil bhakti)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: Which saint is associated with the Virashaiva (Lingayat) tradition of twelfth-century Karnataka?
explanation: The Virashaiva tradition in Karnataka was initiated by Basavanna and his companions. Its followers, the Lingayats, worship Shiva in the form of a linga and reject caste distinctions and the supremacy of the Brahmanas.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6 (Bhakti-Sufi Traditions), section on the Virashaiva tradition in Karnataka

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: In 1604, the compositions of Guru Nanak, Baba Farid, Ravidas and Kabir were compiled as the Adi Granth Sahib by:
explanation: Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth Sahib in 1604. Guru Angad had earlier compiled Guru Nanak's compositions in the Gurmukhi script, and Guru Gobind Singh later added the compositions of Guru Tegh Bahadur to create the Guru Granth Sahib.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6 (Bhakti-Sufi Traditions), section on Baba Guru Nanak and the Sikh tradition (nirguna bhakti)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, whose khanqah was at Delhi, belonged to which Sufi silsila?
explanation: The Chishti silsila was the most influential Sufi order in northern India. Shaikh Muinuddin Chishti of Ajmer, Baba Farid and Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi were among its leading saints.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6 (Bhakti-Sufi Traditions), section on the Sufi silsilas (Chishtis in the subcontinent)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: Which early Sufi mystic was executed for declaring 'Ana'l Haqq' (I am the Truth), a claim that the orthodox regarded as blasphemy?
explanation: Mansur al-Hallaj, a tenth-century Sufi mystic, was executed for declaring 'Ana'l Haqq', as the orthodox took it to mean a claim of identity with God. Rabia was a woman mystic who stressed divine love, and Hasan al-Basri was an early ascetic Sufi.
ncert_ref: Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6 (Bhakti-Sufi Traditions), section on the Sufi beliefs and practices (early Sufis)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: The hymns composed by the Alvars, the Vaishnava saints of the Tamil country, were compiled in a collection known as the:
explanation: The Alvars were devotees of Vishnu, and their compositions were compiled in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham (Four Thousand Sacred Compositions), often described as the Tamil Veda. The Tevaram holds the hymns of the Nayanars, the devotees of Shiva, and the Bijak is a collection of Kabir's verses.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, section on the early traditions of bhakti (Alvars and Nayanars)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: Which of the following was a feature of the Virashaiva (Lingayat) tradition that arose in twelfth-century Karnataka?

options.text: Acceptance of the Dharmashastra rules of caste and ritual pollution
Worship of Vishnu in his incarnations
Wearing a linga on the body as a mark of devotion to Shiva
Faith in the theory of rebirth as the basis of salvation

explanation: Followers of Basavanna worshipped Shiva in the form of a linga, which they wore on the body, usually in a small case on the left shoulder. They challenged caste, the idea of ritual pollution and the Dharmashastras, and questioned the theory of rebirth.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, section on the Virashaiva tradition in Karnataka (Basavanna)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: Which of the following Sufi saints is associated with the dargah at Ajmer?
explanation: The dargah at Ajmer is that of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti, the best known saint of the Chishti silsila in India, and Akbar visited it repeatedly. Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya's dargah is at Delhi and Baba Farid is linked with Ajodhan in the Punjab.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, section on the Sufi silsilas (the Chishtis in the subcontinent)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: In Sufism, the lineage of spiritual masters that links a teacher through a chain of predecessors back to the Prophet is called a:
explanation: Silsila literally means a chain and stands for the unbroken spiritual genealogy of Sufi masters traced back to the Prophet. A khanqah is the hospice where a master lived with disciples, a dargah is the shrine of a saint and sama is the recital of devotional music.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, section on Sufi silsilas

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: The Adi Granth Sahib compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604 includes the compositions of Baba Guru Nanak along with those of saints such as:
explanation: Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth Sahib in 1604 from the compositions of Baba Guru Nanak, the later Sikh Gurus and saints such as Baba Farid, Ravidas and Kabir. Guru Gobind Singh later added the compositions of Guru Tegh Bahadur, and the work came to be known as the Guru Granth Sahib.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, section on Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Appar
(B) Basavanna
(C) Mirabai
(D) Baba Farid

List-II
(I) Chishti Sufi whose verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib
(II) Nayanar saint of the Tamil country
(III) Leader of the Virashaiva movement in Karnataka
(IV) Devotee of Krishna from Rajasthan

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Appar was one of the Nayanars, the Shaiva saints of the Tamil country. Basavanna led the Virashaiva movement in Karnataka, Mirabai was a devotee of Krishna from Rajasthan and Baba Farid was a Chishti Sufi whose verses were included in the Guru Granth Sahib.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, sections on Alvars and Nayanars, Virashaivas, Sufi silsilas and Mirabai

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem:
Consider the following statements about Kabir.

(A) Some of his verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib.
(B) He spoke of the Supreme Being as formless and rejected idol worship.
(C) He is the author of the Ramcharitmanas.
(D) Collections such as the Bijak preserve compositions attributed to him.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Kabir's verses were preserved in the Kabir Bijak and the Kabir Granthavali and some are included in the Guru Granth Sahib. He described the divine as formless and rejected idol worship and ritual. The Ramcharitmanas was composed by Tulsidas.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, section on Kabir

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem:
Arrange the following religious thinkers and saints in chronological order, from the earliest to the latest.

(A) Basavanna
(B) Guru Nanak
(C) Shankara
(D) Ramanuja

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Shankara belonged to the eighth century, Ramanuja to the eleventh century and Basavanna to the twelfth century. Guru Nanak was born in 1469, so the order is Shankara, Ramanuja, Basavanna, Guru Nanak.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, sections on philosophy and devotion, the Virashaivas and Baba Guru Nanak

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 by:
explanation: Harihara and Bukka founded the Vijayanagara Empire in 1336 and established the Sangama dynasty. Saluva Narasimha and Krishnadeva Raya belonged to later dynasties, and Rama Raya was the chief minister who led the army at Rakshasi-Tangadi in 1565.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 7 An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara, introduction and section on the Rayas and Nayakas

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: In 1565 the Vijayanagara army under Rama Raya was defeated at Rakshasi-Tangadi (Talikota) by the combined forces of:
explanation: At Rakshasi-Tangadi, also called Talikota, the armies of the Sultanates of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda defeated Rama Raya. Vijayanagara was then sacked and abandoned.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 7 An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara, section on the dynasties and the sack of the city (1565)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: In the Vijayanagara Empire, the amara-nayakas were:

options.text: priests who managed the endowments and festivals of the Hampi temples
military commanders who held territories from the raya and collected taxes there
foreign merchants who supplied horses and luxury goods to the royal court
village accountants who kept the records of land and revenue for the empire

explanation: The amara-nayakas were military commanders given territories to govern by the raya. They collected taxes from peasants, craftspersons and traders, kept part of the revenue and maintained a contingent of horses and elephants. The system drew on features of the iqta system of the Delhi Sultanate.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 7 An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara, section on the amara-nayaka system

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: The Mahanavami dibba in the royal centre of Vijayanagara was:

options.text: a stepped tank used for the ritual bathing of the royal family
a stable for the royal elephants kept at the royal centre
a hall where the king met his council of ministers
a massive platform used for royal ceremonies and display of power

explanation: The Mahanavami dibba was a massive platform in the royal centre. Rituals of the Mahanavami festival, the Dussehra or Navaratri of the Vijayanagara court, were performed there and the king displayed his prestige and power. The stepped tank, elephant stables and the Lotus Mahal are separate structures.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 7 An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara, section on the royal centre (Mahanavami dibba)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Virupaksha temple
(B) Hazara Rama temple
(C) Vitthala temple
(D) Lotus Mahal

List-II
(I) Building named by British travellers, probably a council chamber
(II) Temple with a stone chariot in its complex
(III) Temple of Shiva linked with the local goddess Pampadevi
(IV) Temple with Ramayana scenes carved on its walls, probably used by the royal family

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: The Virupaksha temple is the Shiva temple tied to Pampadevi. The Hazara Rama temple has Ramayana panels and was probably the royal family's shrine. The Vitthala temple has the well-known stone chariot, and the Lotus Mahal got its name from British travellers and was probably a council chamber.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 7 An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara, sections on the royal centre and the sacred centre

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: In Mughal India, peasants who cultivated land in a village other than the one in which they lived, on a contractual basis, were known as:
explanation: Pahi-kashta were non-resident cultivators who belonged to another village but cultivated land elsewhere on a contractual basis. Khud-kashta were resident cultivators of their own village. Muzarian is a general term for peasants, and the qanungo was a keeper of revenue records.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 8 Peasants, Zamindars and the State, section on peasants and agricultural production

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: In Mughal land classification, land that was left fallow for three to four years was called:
explanation: Polaj was land cultivated every year, parauti was left fallow for a short time to recover fertility, chachar was fallow for three to four years and banjar was uncultivated for five years or more.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 8 Peasants, Zamindars and the State, section on land revenue and the classification of land

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: The Ain-i Akbari, written by Abu'l Fazl, forms the third volume of the:
explanation: Abu'l Fazl's Akbarnama has three books, of which the first two are chronicles and the third is the Ain-i Akbari, a detailed account of the administration, revenue system and agrarian conditions of Akbar's empire. The Padshahnama belongs to Shah Jahan's reign and the Baburnama is Babur's memoir.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 8 Peasants, Zamindars and the State, section on the Ain-i Akbari as a source

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem:
Consider the following statements about the village in Mughal India.

(A) The village panchayat was headed by a headman known as the muqaddam or mandal.
(B) The panchayat could impose fines, and expulsion from the community was among its severest punishments.
(C) The village accountant, known as the patwari, kept records of the village.
(D) The panchayat functioned only in villages inhabited by a single caste.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: The panchayat, an assembly of village elders, was headed by the muqaddam or mandal. It could fine offenders and expel them from the community, and the patwari kept the village records. Panchayats also worked in mixed-caste villages, where they were heterogeneous bodies, so statement (D) is wrong.
ncert_ref: Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 8 Peasants, Zamindars and the State, section on the village panchayat

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I (Mughal classification of land)
(A) Polaj
(B) Parauti
(C) Chachar
(D) Banjar
List-II (Description)
(I) Land that lay fallow for three or four years
(II) Land left uncultivated for five years or more
(III) Land cultivated every year and never left fallow
(IV) Land left out of cultivation for a short time to recover its strength
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Polaj was land cultivated every year for each crop in succession and never left fallow. Parauti was left out of cultivation for a short time to recover its strength. Chachar had lain fallow for three or four years, and banjar was uncultivated for five years or more.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 8 (Peasants, Zamindars and the State), section 'Peasants and agricultural production' (land categories in the Ain-i-Akbari)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem:
Consider the following statements about the Mughal countryside (c. sixteenth-seventeenth centuries):
(A) Khud-kashta were peasants who cultivated land in the village where they resided.
(B) The village panchayat was headed by a headman known as the muqaddam or mandal.
(C) Pahi-kashta were resident peasants who held hereditary rights over village lands.
(D) Jama was the amount actually collected by the state, and hasil was the amount assessed.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Khud-kashta were resident cultivators, and the village panchayat was headed by the muqaddam or mandal, so (A) and (B) are correct. Pahi-kashta were non-resident peasants who cultivated land belonging to other villages on a contractual basis, so (C) is wrong. Jama was the amount assessed and hasil the amount actually collected, so (D) reverses the terms.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 8 (Peasants, Zamindars and the State), sections 'The village community' and 'Land revenue system'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
stem: In Mughal sources, crops such as cotton and sugarcane, which brought in more revenue to the state, were called:
explanation: Jins-i-kamil, literally 'perfect crops', was the term for crops such as cotton and sugarcane. The Mughal state encouraged their cultivation because they fetched more revenue. Khud-kashta and pahi-kashta are types of peasants, and polaj is a category of land.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 8 (Peasants, Zamindars and the State), section 'Peasants and agricultural production'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: The Permanent Settlement, which fixed the revenue demand on the zamindars of Bengal in 1793, was introduced by:
explanation: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal in 1793 under Lord Cornwallis. The Company fixed the revenue to be paid by each zamindar permanently, so that the demand would not be raised later. Wellesley is linked with the Subsidiary Alliance and Dalhousie with the Doctrine of Lapse.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 9 (Colonialism and the Countryside), section 'Bengal and the Zamindars'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: Under the 'sunset law' of the Permanent Settlement in Bengal, what happened if a zamindar failed to pay the revenue demand by the specified date?

options.text: The date was extended by a full year without penalty
His estate could be put up for auction
The revenue demand was halved for the next year
His revenue demand was doubled and his estate was left with him

explanation: The Permanent Settlement required zamindars to pay the fixed revenue punctually. If the payment was not made by sunset on the specified date, the estate was liable to be auctioned. Many zamindars lost their estates in this way, as with the large Burdwan estate in 1797.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 9 (Colonialism and the Countryside), section 'Bengal and the Zamindars' (the problem of regular revenue, the sunset law)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: In 1832, a large area of the Rajmahal hills was demarcated as Damin-i-Koh, where the group encouraged to settle as plough cultivators was the:
explanation: The British saw the Santhals as ideal settlers who could clear forests and take up settled plough agriculture. In 1832 they demarcated the Damin-i-Koh in the Rajmahal hills and invited the Santhals to live there. The Paharias, who practised shifting cultivation, were pushed deeper into the hills.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 9 (Colonialism and the Countryside), section 'The hoe and the plough' (Santhals and Damin-i-Koh)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: The cotton boom in the Bombay Deccan in the early 1860s was mainly caused by:

options.text: the American Civil War, which disrupted cotton supplies to Britain
the Limitation Law of 1859, which lowered the cost of credit
the extension of the Permanent Settlement to Bombay
the reduction of the revenue demand after the Revolt of 1857

explanation: Before the American Civil War (1861-65), Britain imported most of its cotton from the United States. When the war disrupted these supplies, British manufacturers turned to India, and cotton exports from Bombay and the Deccan rose sharply. The Permanent Settlement was never extended to Bombay, where ryotwari prevailed.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 9 (Colonialism and the Countryside), section on the Deccan riots (the cotton boom)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Consider the following statements about rural India under colonial rule:
(A) Jotedars were rich peasants who controlled large areas of land in many villages of north Bengal.
(B) Under the Permanent Settlement, the revenue demand was revised upward every ten years.
(C) The Paharias practised shifting cultivation, whereas the Santhals took to settled plough agriculture in the Rajmahal hills.
(D) The Santhal rebellion of 1855-56 was led by Birsa Munda.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Jotedars were powerful rich peasants in north Bengal, and the Paharias and Santhals followed shifting and plough cultivation respectively, so (A) and (C) are correct. The Permanent Settlement fixed the revenue demand permanently, so (B) is wrong. The Santhal rebellion was led by Sido and Kanhu, not Birsa Munda, so (D) is wrong.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 9 (Colonialism and the Countryside), sections 'Bengal and the Zamindars' and 'The hoe and the plough'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) The Deccan riots in Poona and Ahmednagar
(B) The Santhal rebellion
(C) The introduction of the Permanent Settlement in Bengal
(D) The demarcation of the Damin-i-Koh
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793. The Damin-i-Koh was demarcated in 1832, the Santhal rebellion broke out in 1855-56, and the Deccan riots took place in 1875. The correct order is therefore (C), (D), (B), (A).
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 9 (Colonialism and the Countryside), timeline and sections on Bengal, the Santhals and the Deccan riots

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: The revolt of 1857 began on 10 May 1857 with a rising of sepoys at:
explanation: The revolt began as a mutiny of the sepoys of the Bengal Army, starting at Meerut on 10 May 1857. The sepoys then marched to Delhi, which they reached the next day. Kanpur and Lucknow joined the revolt later.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10 (Rebels and the Raj), section 'Pattern of the rebellion'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: After reaching Delhi from Meerut, the rebel sepoys proclaimed which person the leader of the revolt?
explanation: The sepoys who reached Delhi on 11 May 1857 gathered at the Red Fort and asked the aged Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar to bless the revolt. He accepted the leadership, which gave the rebellion a wider political legitimacy. Nana Sahib led the revolt at Kanpur and Birjis Qadr at Lucknow.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10 (Rebels and the Raj), section 'Pattern of the rebellion' (Delhi)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: Which Nawab of Awadh was removed by the British in 1856 and sent into exile in Calcutta?
explanation: In 1856 the British annexed Awadh, claiming it was misgoverned, and removed Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, who was exiled to Calcutta. His removal angered the people of Awadh and many sepoys, who came from the region. Birjis Qadr was his young son, who was proclaimed Nawab during the revolt.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10 (Rebels and the Raj), section on Awadh and the policies of the Company

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: Which of the following states was annexed by Lord Dalhousie in 1848 under the Doctrine of Lapse?
explanation: Under the Doctrine of Lapse, a state could be annexed if its ruler died without a natural male heir. Satara was annexed in 1848, and Nagpur and Jhansi followed in the early 1850s. Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of misgovernment, not under the Doctrine of Lapse.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10 (Rebels and the Raj), section on the policies of the Company (Doctrine of Lapse)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: In 1857 the sepoys were angered by the rumour that the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle were greased with the fat of:
explanation: The rumour spread that the cartridges, which had to be bitten open, were greased with cow and pig fat. This offended both Hindu and Muslim sepoys, who saw it as a plot to destroy their religion. The rumour was a major immediate cause of the revolt.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10 (Rebels and the Raj), section 'Pattern of the rebellion' (rumours and prophecies)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I (Leader of the revolt of 1857)
(A) Rani Lakshmibai
(B) Nana Sahib
(C) Kunwar Singh
(D) Birjis Qadr
List-II (Centre of the revolt)
(I) Lucknow
(II) Jhansi
(III) Arrah in Bihar
(IV) Kanpur
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Rani Lakshmibai led the rebels at Jhansi, and Nana Sahib, the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, at Kanpur. Kunwar Singh, a local zamindar, led the revolt around Arrah in Bihar. Birjis Qadr, the young son of Wajid Ali Shah, was proclaimed Nawab at Lucknow.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10 (Rebels and the Raj), sections 'Pattern of the rebellion' and on Awadh

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) The sepoys of Meerut rise in revolt
(B) The British annex Awadh
(C) An Act of Parliament transfers the Company's powers to the British Crown
(D) The British recapture Delhi
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Awadh was annexed in 1856. The sepoys revolted at Meerut in May 1857, and the British recaptured Delhi in September 1857. In 1858 the British Parliament passed an Act transferring the powers of the East India Company to the Crown, so the order is (B), (A), (D), (C).
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10 (Rebels and the Raj), sections 'Pattern of the rebellion' and 'Repression' and the timeline

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Consider the following statements about the revolt of 1857:
(A) Nana Sahib joined the revolt after the British refused to continue the pension of the late Peshwa Baji Rao II to him.
(B) The Subsidiary Alliance system was introduced by Lord Dalhousie.
(C) The Azamgarh Proclamation of 1857 appealed to both Hindus and Muslims to rise against the British.
(D) Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried by the British and exiled to Rangoon after the recapture of Delhi.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Nana Sahib, the adopted son of Baji Rao II, was denied the Peshwa's pension. The Azamgarh Proclamation addressed both Hindus and Muslims, and Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to Rangoon after Delhi fell, so (A), (C) and (D) are correct. The Subsidiary Alliance was introduced by Lord Wellesley, not Dalhousie, so (B) is wrong.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10 (Rebels and the Raj), sections 'Pattern of the rebellion', 'What the rebels wanted' and 'Repression'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: After returning to India from South Africa in 1915, whom did Mahatma Gandhi regard as his political mentor?
explanation: Gandhi returned to India in January 1915 and looked to the moderate Congress leader Gopal Krishna Gokhale as his political guru. Tilak and Besant belonged to the Home Rule leadership, and Naoroji was an older Congress veteran.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section 'A Leader Announces Himself'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I (Gandhi's early campaign)
(A) Champaran
(B) Kheda
(C) Ahmedabad
(D) Rowlatt Satyagraha
List-II (Issue)
(I) Wages of mill workers
(II) Detention without trial
(III) Forced cultivation of indigo by planters
(IV) Remission of land revenue after crop failure
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: In Champaran (1917) Gandhi took up the case of peasants forced by planters to grow indigo. In Kheda (1917-18) peasants sought revenue remission after crop failure, in Ahmedabad (1918) mill workers fought for better wages, and the Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919) opposed detention without trial.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, sections 'A Leader Announces Himself' and 'The Rowlatt Satyagraha'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: In April 1919 Mahatma Gandhi launched a nationwide satyagraha against which one of the following laws?
explanation: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed the government to detain political prisoners for two years without trial and to curb civil liberties. Gandhi called a hartal on 6 April 1919 against it, beginning the Rowlatt Satyagraha.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section 'The Rowlatt Satyagraha'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: The Khilafat Movement, which Mahatma Gandhi supported, was launched by Indian Muslims mainly to protest against:

options.text: the partition of Bengal carried out by Lord Curzon in 1905
the Rowlatt Act passed by the Imperial Legislative Council
the separate electorates announced in the Communal Award
the harsh treatment of the Ottoman Khalifa after the First World War

explanation: After the First World War the Ottoman Sultan, regarded by many Muslims as the Khalifa, was treated harshly by the victorious Allies. Leaders such as Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali launched the Khilafat Movement, and Gandhi saw in it a chance for Hindu-Muslim unity.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section 'The Non-Cooperation Movement' (Khilafat issue)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Consider the following statements about the Non-Cooperation Movement.
(A) It included the surrender of titles and the boycott of law courts, schools and legislative councils.
(B) Gandhi withdrew it in February 1922 after the violence at Chauri Chaura.
(C) It was launched after the Dandi March of 1930.
(D) It was linked with the Khilafat issue to bring Hindus and Muslims together.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Non-Cooperation (1920-22) involved surrendering titles and boycotting courts, schools, councils and foreign cloth, and it was tied to the Khilafat cause. Gandhi called it off after the Chauri Chaura violence of February 1922. Statement (C) is wrong because the Dandi March belongs to 1930, the Civil Disobedience Movement.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section 'The Non-Cooperation Movement'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Arrange the following events in chronological order.
(A) Chauri Chaura incident
(B) Lahore Congress session demanding Purna Swaraj
(C) Rowlatt Satyagraha
(D) Dandi March
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: The Rowlatt Satyagraha was in 1919, the Chauri Chaura incident in February 1922, the Lahore session demanding Purna Swaraj in December 1929, and the Dandi March in March-April 1930. The correct order is therefore (C), (A), (B), (D).
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, sections on the Rowlatt Satyagraha, Non-Cooperation and the Salt Satyagraha

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Assertion (A): Mahatma Gandhi chose salt as the symbol of his campaign against colonial rule in 1930.
Reason (R): Salt was consumed in every household, rich and poor alike, and the tax on it was felt by all.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

explanation: Gandhi saw salt as a unifying symbol because everyone used it, so the salt tax and the government monopoly hurt every Indian. Both statements are true, and R explains why salt was chosen.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section 'The Salt Satyagraha'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Consider the following statements about the Salt March.
(A) The march began at Dandi and ended at Sabarmati Ashram.
(B) Gandhi wrote to Viceroy Irwin about his demands before starting the march.
(C) Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi on 6 April 1930.
(D) The Salt March marked the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Gandhi wrote to Viceroy Irwin in January 1930 and set out from Sabarmati Ashram on 12 March 1930. He reached Dandi and broke the salt law on 6 April, opening the Civil Disobedience Movement. Statement (A) reverses the route, so it is wrong.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section 'The Salt Satyagraha'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: Under the Poona Pact of September 1932, the Depressed Classes were given:

options.text: separate electorates, as proposed in the Communal Award of 1932
reserved seats in the legislatures, to be voted in by the general electorate
members nominated to the legislatures by the Viceroy and the Governors
no reserved seats at all in the provincial or central legislatures

explanation: Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for the Depressed Classes, and Gandhi fasted against the idea. The Poona Pact gave reserved seats in the provincial and central councils but the candidates were to be elected by the general electorate.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section on Civil Disobedience, the Round Table Conferences and the Poona Pact

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: The call of 'Do or Die' by Mahatma Gandhi is associated with which one of the following movements?
explanation: In his speech at the Bombay meeting of the All India Congress Committee in August 1942, Gandhi gave the mantra 'Do or Die' for the Quit India Movement. Leaders were arrested soon after, and the movement spread without central direction.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section 'Quit India and Later'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Arrange the following in chronological order.
(A) Quit India Movement
(B) Poona Pact
(C) Gandhi-Irwin Pact
(D) Second Round Table Conference in London
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed in March 1931, after which Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in London in late 1931. The Poona Pact followed in September 1932, and the Quit India Movement came in 1942. The order is (C), (D), (B), (A).
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, sections on the Salt Satyagraha, the Round Table Conferences and Quit India

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: At which session of the Indian National Congress, held in December 1929, was complete independence (Purna Swaraj) declared to be the goal?
explanation: The Lahore session, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, declared Purna Swaraj as the goal of the Congress. It decided that 26 January 1930 would be observed as Independence Day.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 13 Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section 'The Salt Satyagraha' (Lahore session and Purna Swaraj)

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly of India?
explanation: B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee that prepared the draft Constitution. Rajendra Prasad was the President of the Constituent Assembly.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 15 Framing the Constitution, section 'The Constituent Assembly'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: The Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru in the Constituent Assembly on 13 December 1946 envisaged India as:

options.text: a Dominion within the British Commonwealth
a confederation of provinces with no common centre
a union of princely states under the British Crown

explanation: Nehru's Objectives Resolution proclaimed India an Independent Sovereign Republic and promised justice, equality and freedom to all its people. It became the guiding framework for the Constitution.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 15 Framing the Constitution, section 'The Vision of the Constituent Assembly'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I (Member of the Constituent Assembly)
(A) Jaipal Singh
(B) K. Santhanam
(C) N. G. Ranga
(D) B. R. Ambedkar
List-II (Stand taken)
(I) Warned of political equality existing alongside social and economic inequality
(II) Argued that tribals needed protection from long-standing exploitation
(III) Argued that the Centre was too powerful and the states needed greater powers
(IV) Argued that the real minorities were the poor and downtrodden masses
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Jaipal Singh spoke for the tribals, K. Santhanam argued for stronger states against an over-powerful Centre, and N. G. Ranga held that the poor were the true minorities. Ambedkar's closing speech warned of a life of contradictions.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 15 Framing the Constitution, sections on protecting minority rights, the Centre and the States, and the concluding debates

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Consider the following statements about the Constituent Assembly.
(A) Its members were elected indirectly by the provincial legislative assemblies in 1946.
(B) The Muslim League members took part in it from its first session in December 1946.
(C) Rajendra Prasad was its President.
(D) The Objectives Resolution was moved in it by Jawaharlal Nehru.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: The members were elected by the provincial assemblies in 1946, Rajendra Prasad became President, and Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution. The Muslim League boycotted the Assembly, so statement (B) is wrong.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 15 Framing the Constitution, section 'The Constituent Assembly'

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: In his concluding speech to the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949, B. R. Ambedkar said that India was entering a 'life of contradictions' because:

options.text: adult franchise had been limited to men who owned property
political equality was granted while social and economic inequality persisted
the Centre had been made too weak to hold the country together
separate electorates for minorities had been retained in the Constitution

explanation: Ambedkar said that from 26 January 1950 India would have equality in politics (one man, one vote) but continue to have inequality in social and economic life. He urged that this contradiction be removed soon.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Ch. 15 Framing the Constitution, closing section on the Assembly's last debates

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem:
Assertion (A): Mahatma Gandhi favoured Hindustani as the national language of India.
Reason (R): Gandhi believed that Hindustani, a blend of Hindi and Urdu, was understood only by the educated elite.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

explanation: Gandhi held that Hindustani, a mixture of Hindi and Urdu, was a language understood by common people across the country and so should be the national language. The assertion is true, but the reason contradicts his view.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Framing the Constitution, discussion of the language question

subject: history
unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
stem: The Constituent Assembly of India held its first meeting on:
explanation: The Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946. It adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, which came into effect on 26 January 1950.
ncert_ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Framing the Constitution, section on the Constituent Assembly

subject: political_science
stem: The demand for the creation of Pakistan made by the Muslim League before 1947 was based on the:
explanation: The Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, argued that Hindus and Muslims were two separate nations and so needed separate homelands. This two-nation theory was the basis of the demand for Pakistan and of the Partition of 1947. Paramountcy, subsidiary alliance and lapse were British policies towards Indian states.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.1 Challenges of Nation Building, section 'Challenges for the new nation' (Partition and the two-nation theory)

subject: political_science
stem: Which leader of the North-West Frontier Province, popularly known as the 'Frontier Gandhi', opposed the two-nation theory?
explanation: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the undisputed leader of the North-West Frontier Province, opposed the two-nation theory. His voice was ultimately ignored and the province was made part of Pakistan. Liaquat Ali Khan was a Muslim League leader.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.1 Challenges of Nation Building, section 'Challenges for the new nation' (the Partition and the North-West Frontier Province)

subject: political_science
stem: By signing the Instrument of Accession, the rulers of the princely states that joined India agreed to hand over which of the following subjects to the Government of India?
explanation: Under the Instrument of Accession, a princely state that joined India transferred defence, external affairs and communications to the Union. The other matters stayed with the state for the time being. Most rulers signed it before or soon after 15 August 1947.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.1 Challenges of Nation Building, section 'Integration of Princely States'

subject: political_science
stem: Which princely state wanted to remain independent and was brought into the Indian Union after a military operation in September 1948?
explanation: The Nizam of Hyderabad wanted an independent status and entered into a standstill agreement with India. When negotiations failed, the Indian army moved in during September 1948 and Hyderabad was integrated. Junagadh and Manipur were integrated in other ways.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.1 Challenges of Nation Building, section 'Integration of Princely States' (Hyderabad)

subject: political_science
stem:
Arrange the following events in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) Passing of the States Reorganisation Act
(B) Death of Potti Sriramulu after a fast demanding a separate Andhra state
(C) Appointment of the States Reorganisation Commission
(D) Division of the Bombay State into Maharashtra and Gujarat
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Potti Sriramulu died in December 1952 after a long fast, which led to the creation of Andhra in 1953. The States Reorganisation Commission was appointed in 1953 and its recommendations led to the States Reorganisation Act of 1956. Bombay State was divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat in 1960.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.1 Challenges of Nation Building, section 'Reorganisation of States'

subject: political_science
stem:
Consider the following statements about the Partition of India in 1947.
(A) Punjab and Bengal were themselves divided because they had large areas in which non-Muslims were in a majority.
(B) Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the leader of the North-West Frontier Province, supported the two-nation theory.
(C) In Punjab and Bengal, partition on the basis of religious majority was done at the district or even lower level.
(D) The Partition did not lead to any large-scale migration of people.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Punjab and Bengal had large non-Muslim areas, so the two provinces were themselves divided, and the division followed religious majority at the district or even lower level. Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan opposed the two-nation theory. The Partition caused one of the largest and most tragic forced migrations in history.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.1 Challenges of Nation Building, section 'Challenges for the new nation' (Partition and displacement)

subject: political_science
stem: Who was the first Chief Election Commissioner of India, under whom the first general elections of 1951-52 were conducted?
explanation: Sukumar Sen was the first Chief Election Commissioner and he conducted the first general elections of 1951-52 for the Lok Sabha and the State Assemblies. The elections were held under universal adult franchise on a very large scale. The other names are later Chief Election Commissioners.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.2 Era of One-Party Dominance, section 'Challenge of building democracy' / 'First general elections'

subject: political_science
stem: Which party, formed in 1959, opposed land ceilings, cooperative farming and state trading, and favoured free private enterprise?
explanation: The Swatantra Party was formed in August 1959 under leaders such as C. Rajagopalachari and Minoo Masani. It criticised state-led planning and called for a reduced role for the government in the economy. The Praja Socialist Party and the Communist Party of India favoured a larger role for the state.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.2 Era of One-Party Dominance, section 'Emergence of opposition parties' (Swatantra Party)

subject: political_science
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I (Leader)
(A) Syama Prasad Mukherjee
(B) C. Rajagopalachari
(C) B. R. Ambedkar
(D) E. M. S. Namboodiripad
List-II (Association)
(I) Swatantra Party
(II) Scheduled Castes Federation
(III) Bharatiya Jana Sangh
(IV) Head of the first Communist government in Kerala, 1957
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Syama Prasad Mukherjee was the founder-leader of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh (1951) and C. Rajagopalachari was a founder of the Swatantra Party (1959). B. R. Ambedkar led the Scheduled Castes Federation, and E. M. S. Namboodiripad headed the Communist government that took office in Kerala in 1957.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.2 Era of One-Party Dominance, sections 'Emergence of opposition parties' and 'Congress dominance'

subject: political_science
stem: Which party formed the government in Kerala in 1957, which the Union Government dismissed in 1959 using Article 356?
explanation: In 1957 the Communist Party of India won the Kerala Assembly elections and E. M. S. Namboodiripad became Chief Minister. It was the first time a Communist government came to power in India through democratic elections. The Union Government dismissed it in 1959 under Article 356, a step widely criticised.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.2 Era of One-Party Dominance, section 'Congress dominance' (Kerala 1957)

subject: political_science
stem:
Assertion (A): In the first general election of 1951-52, the Congress won about three-fourths of the Lok Sabha seats while securing less than half of the votes cast.
Reason (R): India adopted the first-past-the-post system, in which the candidate who gets more votes than any other candidate in a constituency is declared elected.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

explanation: The Congress won 364 of the 489 Lok Sabha seats, about 74 per cent, with roughly 45 per cent of the votes. Under the first-past-the-post system the votes of the other parties were divided and brought them few seats. So the system is the reason why the vote share was converted into a much larger seat share.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.2 Era of One-Party Dominance, section 'Nature of Congress dominance' (first-past-the-post and seat share)

subject: political_science
stem: Which of the following statements about the first general election of India (1951-52) is NOT correct?

options.text: The Lok Sabha and the State Assembly elections were held together.
The Election Commission, headed by the Chief Election Commissioner, conducted the elections.
Every adult citizen, irrespective of caste, class, religion or gender, was given the right to vote.
Only literate citizens who owned property were allowed to vote.

explanation: India adopted universal adult franchise for the first election, so there was no educational or property qualification for voting. The elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies were held together under the Election Commission headed by Sukumar Sen.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.2 Era of One-Party Dominance, section 'Challenge of building democracy' / 'First general elections'

subject: political_science
stem: In which year was the Planning Commission of India set up?
explanation: The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950 by the Government of India. The First Five Year Plan began in 1951 and the Second Five Year Plan in 1956. It was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.3 Politics of Planned Development, section 'Planning Commission'

subject: political_science
stem: The Second Five Year Plan (1956-61), which gave priority to rapid industrialisation and heavy industries, was drafted by a team led by:
explanation: The Second Five Year Plan was prepared under the leadership of the statistician P. C. Mahalanobis and stressed heavy industries and the public sector. K. N. Raj was the economist behind the First Five Year Plan, which stressed agriculture. Charan Singh argued that planning should give priority to agriculture.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.3 Politics of Planned Development, section 'The Second Five Year Plan'

subject: political_science
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I (Term)
(A) Bhoodan
(B) Green Revolution
(C) Bombay Plan
(D) Land ceiling
List-II (Meaning)
(I) Fixing the maximum area of land that one person may own
(II) Voluntary donation of land by landowners to the landless
(III) Use of high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation to raise foodgrain output
(IV) A 1944 blueprint for a planned economy drawn up by leading industrialists
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: Bhoodan, begun by Vinoba Bhave, asked landowners to donate land voluntarily. The Green Revolution used high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation, and the Bombay Plan of 1944 was drawn up by leading industrialists. A land ceiling fixes the maximum land one person can hold.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.3 Politics of Planned Development, sections 'Planning Commission', 'Green Revolution' and 'Land reforms'

subject: political_science
stem: Which of the following was a consequence of the Green Revolution in India?

options.text: It reduced regional disparities as all states gained equally from it.
It reduced the economic inequalities between rich and poor peasants.
It increased regional disparities, as it was confined mostly to irrigated regions.
It increased India's dependence on imported wheat and rice.

explanation: The Green Revolution raised foodgrain output, but it was mostly confined to areas with assured irrigation such as Punjab and Haryana. As a result it sharpened regional disparities, and it also widened the gap between prosperous farmers and poor peasants.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.3 Politics of Planned Development, section 'Green Revolution'

subject: political_science
stem:
Consider the following statements about planned development in India.
(A) The First Five Year Plan gave priority to agriculture, irrigation and dams.
(B) The Second Five Year Plan emphasised rapid industrialisation, especially heavy industries.
(C) The planners rejected any role for the private sector in the economy.
(D) The Bombay Plan of 1944, drawn up by leading industrialists, wanted the state to take a major initiative in industrial investment.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: The First Plan stressed agriculture, irrigation and dams, and the Second Plan stressed heavy industry. The Bombay Plan of 1944 asked for a major state role in industrial investment. Statement (C) is wrong because India chose a mixed economy in which the private sector kept an important place.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.3 Politics of Planned Development, sections 'Planning Commission', 'The First Five Year Plan' and 'The Second Five Year Plan'

subject: political_science
stem:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) Setting up of the Planning Commission
(B) Replacement of the Planning Commission by NITI Aayog
(C) Launch of the Second Five Year Plan
(D) Preparation of the Bombay Plan by leading industrialists
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
explanation: The Bombay Plan came first, in 1944. The Planning Commission was set up in 1950, the Second Five Year Plan began in 1956, and NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.3 Politics of Planned Development, sections 'Planning Commission' and 'The Second Five Year Plan'

subject: political_science
stem: Which agreement was signed by Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri and President Ayub Khan in January 1966 after the 1965 war between India and Pakistan?
explanation: After the 1965 war between India and Pakistan, the Soviet Union mediated and the Tashkent Agreement was signed in January 1966. Shastri died at Tashkent soon after. The Shimla Agreement was signed in 1972, the Indus Waters Treaty in 1960 and the Lahore Declaration in 1999.
ncert_ref: Class XII Political Science, Politics in India Since Independence, Ch.4 India's External Relations, section 'Wars and peace with Pakistan' / 'Pakistan and the Bangladesh war'

subject: political_science
stem: The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement was held in 1961 in:
explanation: The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement was held in Belgrade in 1961, with Nehru, Tito and Nasser among its founding leaders. Bandung hosted the Afro-Asian conference of 1955 that prepared the ground for it.
